video_title: "It's A Fire Sale" On Gold & Silver Right Now | Matt Piepenburg
gist: Von Greyerz partner Matt Piepenburg argues that 2026's >30% gold and >60% silver drawdown (driven by margin-call liquidations, high real yields and an engineered silver crash) is a 'fire sale', because a private-credit/PE/AI credit crisis plus $40T of US debt at 5%+ cost will force a dovish pivot to QE and yield curve control, likely by 2027. He backs the case with central bank gold accumulation, de-dollarization and real inflation near 10%, and projects $10k-20k gold.

themes.theme: Why gold and silver sold off in 2026

insights.claim: Gold is down more than 30% and silver more than 60% in 2026 after a vertical blow-off top in January (gold near $5,200-5,400, silver near $110-115), a drawdown Piepenburg frames as a normal bull-market shakeout rather than a thesis break.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Size of the drawdown sets the context for a contrarian accumulation case; vertical tops historically correct sharply rather than sideways.
insights.quote: the greater than 30% losses this year in gold and more than 60% in silver, which is extraordinary

insights.claim: Last week's sharp precious-metals drop coincided with a broad liquidation (Anthropic IPO week, worst Dow week in years, Dow below 50,000, a $39B money-market outflow) that Piepenburg attributes to margin calls forcing sale of the most liquid assets, including gold and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: In leverage-driven liquidations gold gets sold alongside risk assets; such forced-selling lows can be entry points for unlevered buyers.
insights.quote: I think it really was a margin call

insights.claim: Margin leverage is extreme: roughly $3.50 of margin leverage for every $1 of cash on hand, which makes cross-asset forced selling more likely on any shock.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Watch margin-debt-to-cash ratios as a fragility gauge; high leverage amplifies drawdowns across all liquid assets.

insights.claim: In a liquidity crunch with rising rates, everything falls except the dollar, which gets bid as collateral for margin; silver is especially rate-sensitive.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Expect dollar strength and precious-metals weakness during acute deleveraging; the regime flips once policy turns dovish.
insights.quote: when you have a liquidity crisis and you have rising rates, everything goes down but the dollar

insights.claim: High nominal and real yields create an opportunity cost for a yieldless asset: investors are choosing long-end Treasuries, investment-grade credit (about $1.9T issued, 6-8% coupons) and below-par tech loans with equity-like total returns over gold.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Gold's headwind is the yield alternative; a fall in real yields (policy pivot) removes it.

insights.claim: Piepenburg claims the late-January silver crash was an engineered price move by COMEX/CME (margin changes) that triggered cascading stop-losses and killed sentiment.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Exchange margin changes can drive violent silver moves independent of fundamentals; size positions to avoid being stopped out.
insights.quote: That was an absolute engineered price, you know, manipulation by the COMEX and the CME

insights.claim: War-related liquidity needs forced countries such as Turkey and Middle East states, even oil-rich ones, to sell their most liquid asset, gold, adding supply this year.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Sovereign forced selling is a temporary supply source that fades once liquidity needs ease.

insights.claim: Of roughly 8 billion ounces of above-ground gold, about 7 billion are held by central banks and big institutions, leaving only 500 million to 1 billion ounces freely traded; retail allocation is under 3% versus about 8% in 1980, so even a small retail shift could move price dramatically.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Thin free float plus low retail allocation means asymmetric upside if retail demand returns.

insights.claim: In the 1970-1980 gold bull market, gold fell more than 20% five times and was cut in half before rising roughly 8x, so deep corrections are consistent with a secular bull.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Use historical drawdown patterns to avoid capitulating in secular uptrends.
insights.quote: gold went down by greater than 20% five times. It got cut in half before it went up by 8x

themes.theme: Credit bubble: private credit, private equity and AI capex

insights.claim: Private credit is mispriced: identical loan books are marked at 90 by one pension fund and 30 by another, and Piepenburg (citing Gundlach) believes the sector is CCC at best, implying fair value around 60.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Avoid or underweight private credit vehicles; pension/insurer exposure is a hidden systemic risk.
insights.quote: Private credits are a bug looking for a windshield

insights.claim: Private credit funds impose gates (around 5% redeemable per quarter) because managers know valuations are inflated; understaffed rating agencies are repeating the 2008 MBS rating failure.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Gated redemption terms signal illiquidity risk; expect markdowns when withdrawals accelerate.

insights.claim: The private equity leveraged-buyout model depended on 0-2% rates that are never coming back; family offices are quietly trying to dump PE and private credit books at discounts because no one trusts the marks.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Expect secondary-market discounts and weak PE returns; secondaries pricing is a stress indicator.
insights.quote: It's based on interest rates being about 0 to 2%. Those rates are never coming back.

insights.claim: AI is the biggest capital misallocation Piepenburg has studied: about $1.1T of hyperscaler capex over two years and around $3T of off-balance-sheet debt, with five hyperscalers responsible for 93% of S&P returns.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Index concentration in AI spenders is a major downside risk for passive equity holders.
insights.quote: that is the biggest misallocation of capital I've ever seen or studied

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are betting heavily on Anthropic and OpenAI, which Piepenburg says have operating losses of $8B and $14B respectively; Google recorded its first cash shortfall since going public in 2004.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Watch hyperscaler free cash flow and funding needs as signs of capex strain.

insights.claim: Using Gundlach's analogy, the AI buildout resembles the 19th-century UK railroad boom, where competitors outspent each other and none ended up profitable.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Overbuilding phases often enrich users, not builders; be skeptical of capex-race winners.
insights.quote: Not one of them made a profit when all was said and done.

insights.claim: AI-related bonds from CoreWeave, Google and SpaceX are trading well below par with widening spreads and falling quarter-over-quarter margins; Piepenburg expects bond investors to eventually revolt against AI debt.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Credit spreads on AI issuers are a leading indicator for AI equity trouble.
insights.quote: eventually bond investors are going to revolt

insights.claim: Piepenburg dismisses the day's Nvidia rally (around 30% in a day, tied to its CEO) as an artificial, speculative move and warns that chasing tops in this market is very dangerous.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Treat parabolic single-day moves in AI leaders as signs of speculative excess rather than confirmation.

themes.theme: Sovereign debt, fiscal dominance and the coming Fed pivot

insights.claim: US public debt has gone from $23T to $40T in six years while its average cost has risen from 0.5% to over 5%; global government debt is up 5x in 25 years ($21T to $115T) while yields hit decade highs.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Rising debt times rising cost is the core arithmetic behind expected monetization and gold upside.
insights.quote: Just six years ago, six years ago, US public debt, government debt was 23 trillion. Today it's 40 trillion.

insights.claim: With about $7.5T in annual costs versus about $5T in tax receipts, the US is in fiscal dominance and cannot sustain a hawkish policy; Piepenburg sees a pivot to rate cuts, yield curve control and outright QE as inevitable.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Position for a dovish pivot (falling real yields, weaker dollar, stronger metals) rather than trying to time it.
insights.quote: at 40 trillion in public debt in the US, we can't sustain a hawkish policy, period

insights.claim: Piepenburg thinks the big dovish pivot is more likely than not by 2027, in line with recent guests Felix Zulauf and Porter Stansberry, but declines to pick a date because he wrongly expected a pivot right after the 2023 bank failures.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: 2027 is the consensus window among hard-money bulls for a major policy rescue; keep exposure without leverage.
insights.quote: It's very likely to happen by 2027

insights.claim: Historical template: QT plus rate hikes broke markets in December 2018, leading to volatility in 2019 and unlimited QE by 2020; 2022 hikes produced the worst nominal stock-and-bond returns since 1871 and then three of the four largest US bank failures in 2023. Piepenburg says today is the same setup.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Treat tightening into high debt as a countdown to a market accident and a policy reversal.
insights.quote: It is exactly the same situation we're in today.

insights.claim: Policymakers are already running 'non-QE QE': Operation Twist 2.0 with more short-end issuance, repo operations, Basel III leniency for banks, and buying back Treasuries Japan was selling; Piepenburg expects this to become outright QE.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Stealth liquidity is a leading signal of the eventual open pivot; track Treasury issuance mix and repo facilities.
insights.quote: They're basically doing non-QE QE now, but it will get to outright QE.

insights.claim: From September 2024 to January 2026 the Fed cut 175bp after hiking 500bp, yet long yields rose; Piepenburg reads this as proof the Fed is losing control of long rates at debt-to-GDP around 100-120%.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Rate cuts alone may not lower long yields, which raises the odds of yield curve control and direct monetization.
insights.quote: he cut by 175 basis points and yields were supposed to go down, but they went up

insights.claim: The Fed's real mandate is protecting the bond market, not inflation or employment, so it will ultimately choose debasement over letting Treasuries break.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: When stress hits Treasuries, expect intervention, which favors hard assets.
insights.quote: the real mandate is the bond market

insights.claim: Possible official tricks such as a gold revaluation, gold-backed long-dated Treasuries (with Judy Shelton at Treasury) and bank stablecoins under the GENIUS Act starting January 18 will not fix the deficit math.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: A gold revaluation is a tail-risk upside catalyst for bullion; stablecoins do not solve the debt problem.
insights.quote: stable coin is not going to save them

insights.claim: Piepenburg expects gold's January all-time highs to be surpassed and projects $10,000-20,000 gold over the longer term.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Explicit long-horizon target from a hard-money bull; it implies multiple-fold upside from current levels.
insights.quote: gold will go to 10 15 20,000 it will

insights.claim: Measured in gold, the S&P 500 is down 40% since its Q4 2021 peak even though it is up 60% in dollars, and US Treasuries have lost 90% against gold over 12 years.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Re-denominate portfolio performance in gold to see real purchasing-power returns.
insights.quote: in the last 12 years, 12 years, you've lost 90% in US Treasuries when measured against gold

insights.claim: Since 2000, gold has compounded at roughly +10% a year against a roughly -10% CAGR for the dollar's purchasing power, in Piepenburg's figures.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Long-run gold CAGR is the benchmark that fiat-denominated returns have to beat.

insights.claim: Real inflation is probably about 10%, not the BLS figure, according to import-export prices (8-9%), John Williams' 1980s-style methodology (10-11%) and Michael Green's annual debt-growth proxy (8-9%). That means junk bonds, below-par AI bonds and 10-year Treasuries all yield negative real returns.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: If true, nominal fixed income is a losing store of value; favor real assets.
insights.quote: Real inflation, if we're being generous, is probably 10%

insights.claim: Governments understate inflation (BLS, the trimmed-median PCE work on Kevin Warsh's task force) so they can run negative real rates and inflate away debt at savers' expense.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Expect financial repression; hold assets that cannot be printed.

insights.claim: The US historically sacrifices the dollar to fix structural problems: in 2001-2008 oil went from about $15 to $145-150. Piepenburg expects a deliberately weaker dollar now to reshore jobs and save the bond market, possibly alongside a gold revaluation.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Policy intent favors a weaker dollar, which supports gold and dollar-denominated real assets.
insights.quote: We're going to squeeze this dollar down to save the bond market and we're going to revalue gold

insights.claim: US broad money supply is up 45% in six years; when debt-to-GDP exceeds 100-120%, rate hikes add to money supply through higher interest payments instead of fighting inflation.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: At high debt loads, hiking is less effective against inflation, which weakens the case for holding cash.

themes.theme: Central bank gold buying and the shift away from the dollar

insights.claim: The People's Bank of China has bought gold for 23 straight months, and central bank buying this year is the highest ever despite low prices: 11 of 12 quarters above 200 tons, with China leading.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Price-insensitive official demand provides a floor and shows long-horizon conviction.
insights.quote: 11 out of 12 quarters at over 200 tons a quarter with China of course leading the way

insights.claim: Central banks are accumulating gold at 5x the pre-2022 pace after the US weaponized the dollar; gold has overtaken US Treasuries in central bank reserves, and the dollar's share of FX reserves has fallen from 80% to under 50%.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: De-dollarization is a structural bid under gold that does not depend on retail sentiment.

insights.claim: Global collateral is shifting from Treasuries and dollars toward gold as a net settlement asset. Piepenburg points to Basel allocated-gold requirements, BIS tier-1 status, net stable funding rules, COMEX outflows and Bessent's talk of monetizing the asset side of the balance sheet. He frames this as the end of dollar hegemony, not the end of the dollar.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Regulatory and official moves toward gold as collateral support a higher long-term price floor.
insights.quote: the global collateral shifts from treasuries and dollars

insights.claim: Wealthy hedge fund managers and bankers who discourage gold at work quietly move their own money into physical gold vaulted in Switzerland, outside the banking system.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Smart-money personal behavior diverges from institutional advice, which suggests gold is under-owned in managed portfolios.

themes.theme: Main Street stress, social unrest and centralization

insights.claim: Consumer stocks such as McDonald's, Home Depot, Lululemon and Chipotle are down 30-40% as the bottom 60-70% of Americans get squeezed, while the top 10% own 85% of stocks.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Consumer discretionary weakness reflects real purchasing-power erosion; be cautious on mass-market consumer names.

insights.claim: Piepenburg cites oil-price inflation acting as a roughly $300B tax on Americans, 15-16 consecutive downward revisions to labor data, and the worst University of Michigan sentiment reading in 50 years as evidence of a weakening economy.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Stacked negative revisions and record-low sentiment raise recession risk and the odds of a dovish pivot.

insights.claim: Debt crises lead to currency crises, then inflation, social unrest and political centralization. Piepenburg points to European street riots and the US affordability-driven 'blue wave', and sees programmable bank stablecoins as the centralization step.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Expect more political volatility and policy shifts toward financial control; consider holding assets outside the banking system.
insights.quote: you always get social unrest because inflation is felt

insights.claim: Von Greyerz's approach is to save in gold and spend in fiat, buying regardless of price because they see metals as a better store of value than paper money; unlevered investors cannot be margin-called or stopped out of their position.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Holding physical metal unlevered for 5-10 years avoids the forced-selling dynamics that drove this year's drawdown.
insights.quote: we save in gold and we spend in fiat

insights.claim: Piepenburg calls the current sell-off a 'fire sale' and says wealthy clients and central banks are buying the dip rather than selling.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Contrarian accumulation signal from high-net-worth flows; dollar-cost averaging into weakness fits this thesis.
insights.quote: It is a fire sale on the metals for those who understand its longer-term direction with conviction.

insights.claim: Even small holdings such as grams of gold or ounces of silver give a large relative advantage, since US retail allocation to gold is under 2.5% and most people own none.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Gradual accumulation of physical metal is accessible to small investors; the edge comes from owning some rather than none.

insights.claim: Piepenburg compares holding gold now to his Brown contemporary Porter Collins' Big Short trade at FrontPoint, where the ABX mortgage index rose while foreclosures surged, so conviction meant holding through adverse marks.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: When fundamentals and price diverge, sizing and staying power matter more than timing.

insights.claim: Physical gold should be held outside the banking system in a safe jurisdiction (Von Greyerz vaults in Zurich and Singapore, minimum CHF 500k; mountain vault, minimum CHF 5M); Piepenburg says a bank is not a safe place to hold gold.
insights.speaker: Matt Piepenburg
insights.so_what: Custody and jurisdiction risk matter for bullion holders; prefer non-bank allocated storage.
